birthplace: New York City, New York, United States
nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; novelist and short-story writer writing in English
literary_identity: American writer whose stories of adolescent alienation and of the Glass family - above all The Catcher in the Rye - made him the most influential and most reclusive American writer of the postwar decades
biography: Jerome David Salinger was born in Manhattan on 1 January 1919, the son of a Jewish importer of cheese and ham and a mother of Scots-Irish descent; he was educated at the McBurney School and at Valley Forge Military Academy, spent a year at New York University and studied briefly at Ursinus College and Columbia, where Whit Burnett's short-story course led to his first sale, 'The Young Folks', to Story in 1940. He served in the US Army from 1942 to 1945, landed in Normandy on D-Day and was present at the liberation of a subcamp of Dachau, and his war experience is behind much of his fiction. 'A Perfect Day for Bananafish' (The New Yorker, 1948) began the Glass family sequence; The Catcher in the Rye (1951) made him famous; Nine Stories (1953), Franny and Zooey (1961) and Raise High the Roof Beam, Carpenters and Seymour: An Introduction (1963) followed, and 'Hapworth 16, 1924' (The New Yorker, 1965) was the last thing he published. He withdrew to Cornish, New Hampshire, avoided publicity for the rest of his life and died there on 27 January 2010.
literary_profile: Fiction: The Catcher in the Rye (1951), Nine Stories (1953), Franny and Zooey (1961), Raise High the Roof Beam, Carpenters and Seymour: An Introduction (1963) and the uncollected 'Hapworth 16, 1924' (1965). Stories of the 1940s, some uncollected in his lifetime, are gathered in Three Early Stories (2014).
stylistic_characteristics: A colloquial, idiomatic first-person voice that catches adolescent speech exactly; dialogue that carries almost all of the action; a habit of sudden religious or mystical intensity inside ordinary conversation; irony that turns to tenderness without warning; the recurring device of the child who is wiser than the adults around her.
intellectual_concerns: Adolescent alienation and the loss of innocence; the phoniness of adult society and the longing for authenticity; war, trauma and what Salinger called 'squalor'; the family as a religious community, above all in the Glass stories; Zen, Vedanta and Christian mysticism; the holiness of the child.
historical_significance: Salinger is the writer through whom the American postwar adolescent found a voice, and The Catcher in the Rye is one of the most widely read and most frequently taught American novels of the century; his stories, particularly 'For Esmé' and the Glass sequence, are central to the criticism of the American short story, and his reclusiveness made him a cultural figure as well as a literary one.
bibliographical_notes: The titles and dates above come from Wikipedia's articles on Salinger and on 'For Esmé', read directly; they were not checked against a bibliography. Installment 10 records only the Norton selection, 'For Esmé—with Love and Squalor' (The New Yorker, 8 April 1950; Nine Stories, 1953); The Catcher in the Rye and the other books have no records, so the bibliography is incomplete.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; novelist, poet and diarist writing in English
literary_identity: American novelist of the Beat Generation, whose spontaneous prose and road narratives - above all On the Road - made the cross-country journey the founding myth of postwar American counterculture
biography: Jean-Louis Lebris de Kérouac was born in Lowell, Massachusetts, on 12 March 1922 to French Canadian parents and grew up speaking joual, learning English at about six. He won a football scholarship to Columbia University, injured his leg, left without a degree, served in the merchant marine and the navy, and met Allen Ginsberg, William Burroughs and Neal Cassady in New York in the mid-1940s. The Town and the City (1950) was his first novel; On the Road, written in 1951 on a continuous roll of paper and published by Viking on 5 September 1957, made him famous. The Subterraneans (1958), The Dharma Bums (1958), Doctor Sax (1959), Maggie Cassidy (1959), Tristessa (1960), Lonesome Traveler (1960), Big Sur (1962), Visions of Gerard (1963), Desolation Angels (1965) and Vanity of Duluoz (1968) followed, with the poetry of Mexico City Blues (1959) and The Scripture of the Golden Eternity (1960). He drank heavily in his last years, lived with his mother and his third wife Stella Sampas, and died at St Petersburg, Florida, on 21 October 1969.
literary_profile: Novels: The Town and the City (1950), On the Road (1957), The Subterraneans (1958), The Dharma Bums (1958), Doctor Sax (1959), Maggie Cassidy (1959), Tristessa (1960), Big Sur (1962), Visions of Gerard (1963), Desolation Angels (1965) and Vanity of Duluoz (1968), with the posthumous Visions of Cody (1972), The Sea Is My Brother (2011) and others. Poetry: Mexico City Blues (1959), The Scripture of the Golden Eternity (1960) and Book of Blues (1995).
stylistic_characteristics: Spontaneous prose: long, paratactic sentences driven by breath and jazz rhythm, with dashes and colons instead of full stops; the deliberate refusal of revision in the manuscripts; a diction that mixes slang, Catholic devotional language, Buddhist terminology and French Canadian speech; the road, the car and the jazz club as recurring settings.
intellectual_concerns: The road, movement and the refusal of settled life; jazz, sex and intoxication as forms of ecstasy; friendship and the search for a father or a brother; Catholic and Buddhist mysticism; the American landscape, its small towns and its dispossessed; the sadness and exhaustion that follow the ecstasy.
historical_significance: Kerouac is the central novelist of the Beat Generation and the writer who gave postwar American prose its most imitated style; On the Road is one of the defining American books of the 1950s, it has been continuously in print and taught as a document of the counterculture, and its manuscript roll is among the best-known objects in American literary history.
bibliographical_notes: The titles and dates above come from Wikipedia's articles on Kerouac and on On the Road, read directly, and from general knowledge; they were not checked against a bibliography. Installment 10 records only the Norton selection, On the Road (Viking, 5 September 1957); the other novels and the poetry have no records, so the bibliography is incomplete.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; novelist, short-story writer and essayist writing in English
literary_identity: American novelist and satirist whose dark comedies of technology, war and American optimism - Cat's Cradle, Slaughterhouse-Five - made him the most widely read counter-cultural novelist of the 1960s
biography: Kurt Vonnegut Jr. was born in Indianapolis on 11 November 1922, the son of an architect; he studied chemistry at Cornell, enlisted in the US Army in 1943, was captured in the Battle of the Bulge and was a prisoner of war in Dresden, where he survived the firebombing in February 1945 in an underground meat locker of a slaughterhouse - the experience behind Slaughterhouse-Five. He took an MA in anthropology at the University of Chicago, worked as a police reporter for the City News Bureau of Chicago and as a public-relations writer for General Electric, and began publishing stories in the Saturday Evening Post and the Magazine of Fantasy and Science Fiction. Player Piano (1952), The Sirens of Titan (1959), Mother Night (1961), Cat's Cradle (1963), God Bless You, Mr. Rosewater (1965), Slaughterhouse-Five (1969), Breakfast of Champions (1973), Slapstick (1976), Jailbird (1979), Deadeye Dick (1982), Galápagos (1985), Bluebeard (1987), Hocus Pocus (1990) and Timequake (1997) are the novels, with the stories of Canary in a Cathouse (1961) and Welcome to the Monkey House (1968), the play Happy Birthday, Wanda June (1970) and the essays of Palm Sunday (1981) and A Man Without a Country (2005). He died in New York on 11 April 2007.
literary_profile: Novels: Player Piano (1952), The Sirens of Titan (1959), Mother Night (1961), Cat's Cradle (1963), God Bless You, Mr. Rosewater (1965), Slaughterhouse-Five (1969), Breakfast of Champions (1973), Slapstick (1976), Jailbird (1979), Deadeye Dick (1982), Galápagos (1985), Bluebeard (1987), Hocus Pocus (1990) and Timequake (1997). Stories: Canary in a Cathouse (1961), Welcome to the Monkey House (1968), Bagombo Snuff Box (1999) and Complete Stories (2017). Non-fiction: Palm Sunday (1981), Fates Worse Than Death (1991), A Man Without a Country (2005) and Armageddon in Retrospect (2008).
stylistic_characteristics: Short, flat, deadpan sentences and very short paragraphs, often of one line; a naive or helpless protagonist moved through events he cannot control; science-fiction devices (time travel, aliens, apocalypse) used as satire; recurring catchphrases ('So it goes'); diagrams, lists and drawings incorporated into the printed text; a sentimental and moralising voice underneath the irony.
intellectual_concerns: War and massacre, above all the bombing of Dresden; technology, automation and the degradation of work; American optimism, consumerism and the religion of success; free will and fatalism; religion invented and institutionalised (Bokononism); loneliness, family and the search for community; death, treated with irony and tenderness at once.
historical_significance: Vonnegut is the most widely read American satirist of the postwar decades and, with Heller and Pynchon, one of the writers through whom the American postmodern novel is taught; Slaughterhouse-Five is a standard text of the anti-war literature of Vietnam-era America, has been adapted for film and stage and has never been out of print, and 'Harrison Bergeron' is one of the most widely anthologised American short stories, a set text in schools for the critique of enforced equality.
bibliographical_notes: The titles and dates above come from Wikipedia's articles on Vonnegut, 'Harrison Bergeron' and Slaughterhouse-Five, read directly; they were not checked against a bibliography. Installment 10 records only the two Norton selections - 'Harrison Bergeron' (The Magazine of Fantasy and Science Fiction, October 1961; Welcome to the Monkey House, 1968) and Slaughterhouse-Five (Delacorte, 31 March 1969); the other novels and the essays have no records, so the bibliography is incomplete.

birthplace: New York City, New York, United States
nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; short-story writer, poet and political activist writing in English
literary_identity: American short-story writer of the Bronx and Greenwich Village, whose talky, digressive, funny stories of mothers, fathers, neighbours and radicals made her the great miniaturist of American city life
biography: Grace Goodside was born in the Bronx, New York, on 11 December 1922, the daughter of Ukrainian Jewish immigrants who had come to the United States in 1906 and who spoke Russian and Yiddish at home; her father, Isaac Goodside, became a doctor. She dropped out of high school at sixteen, attended Hunter College for a year and studied poetry briefly with W. H. Auden at the New School, married the film cameraman Jess Paley in 1942 and had two children, and was active for the rest of her life in the feminist, anti-war and peace movements - she was a member of the War Resisters League and one of the founding members of the Greenwich Village Peace Center. The Little Disturbances of Man (1959), Enormous Changes at the Last Minute (1974) and Later the Same Day (1985) are the three collections, gathered as The Collected Stories (1994), which was a finalist for the Pulitzer Prize and the National Book Award; the poems are collected in Leaning Forward (1985) and Begin Again (2000), and the essays in Just As I Thought (1998). She taught at Columbia, Syracuse and the City College of New York, was Poet Laureate of Vermont from 2003, and died at Thetford, Vermont, on 22 August 2007.
literary_profile: Stories: The Little Disturbances of Man (1959), Enormous Changes at the Last Minute (1974), Later the Same Day (1985) and The Collected Stories (1994). Poetry: Leaning Forward (1985) and Begin Again: Collected Poems (2000). Essays and interviews: Just As I Thought (1998) and Conversations with Grace Paley (1997).
stylistic_characteristics: A talky, digressive, first-person or free indirect voice that reproduces the rhythms of New York speech; very short paragraphs and abrupt transitions; jokes, repetitions and direct addresses to the reader; stories that refuse conventional closure and often end in the middle of a conversation; a mixture of realism and metafictional experiment.
intellectual_concerns: Mothers, fathers, children and the ordinary labour of family life; the Bronx, Greenwich Village and the street as a community; Jewish immigrant inheritance; feminism, abortion, friendship between women; politics and activism, above all the anti-war and peace movements; storytelling itself, and the ethics of the stories we tell about other people.
historical_significance: Paley is one of the most admired American short-story writers of the century and the model for a whole school of voice-driven American fiction; her three collections are small in number and enormous in influence, 'A Conversation with My Father' is among the most discussed American stories of the 1970s, and her combination of formal experiment with political commitment made her a central figure for feminist criticism.
bibliographical_notes: The titles and dates above come from Wikipedia's articles on Paley and on Later the Same Day, read directly, and from the Encyclopedia.com entry on 'A Conversation with My Father'. They were not checked against a bibliography. Installment 10 records only the two Norton selections - 'A Conversation with My Father' (New American Review, 1972; Enormous Changes at the Last Minute, 1974) and 'Zagrowsky Tells' (Mother Jones, May 1985; Later the Same Day, 1985); the other collections, the poems and the essays have no records, so the bibliography is incomplete.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; poet, art curator and critic writing in English
literary_identity: American poet and Museum of Modern Art curator, the liveliest of the New York School poets, whose 'I do this, I do that' lunch poems made the ordinary afternoon the subject of American lyric verse
biography: Francis Russell O'Hara was born in Baltimore on 27 March 1926 and grew up in Grafton, Massachusetts; he studied piano at the New England Conservatory, served as a sonarman in the US Navy in the Pacific, and took his degree at Harvard in 1950, where he met John Ashbery and began publishing in the Harvard Advocate. He took an MA at the University of Michigan, where he won a Hopwood Award, moved to New York in 1951, worked at the front desk of the Museum of Modern Art and rose there to associate curator of painting and sculpture, writing the catalogues of Jackson Pollock and Robert Motherwell and reviews for ArtNews. His books in his lifetime were small gallery and press editions - A City Winter and Other Poems (1952), Oranges: 12 pastorals (1953), Meditations in an Emergency (1957), Odes (1960), Lunch Poems (1964) and Love Poems (Tentative Title) (1965) - and his poetry was assembled after his death in The Collected Poems, edited by Donald Allen (1971), which shared the National Book Award in 1972. He was struck by a jeep on the beach at Fire Island on 24 July 1966 and died the next day at Mastic Beach, Long Island.
literary_profile: Poetry: A City Winter and Other Poems (1952), Oranges: 12 pastorals (1953), Meditations in an Emergency (1957), Odes (1960), Lunch Poems (1964) and Love Poems (Tentative Title) (1965), collected in The Collected Poems of Frank O'Hara, ed. Donald Allen (1971), and in the posthumous selection In Memory of My Feelings (1967). Prose: Jackson Pollock (1959), Art Chronicles 1954-1966 (1975) and the mock manifesto 'Personism' (written 1959, published in Yugen, 1961).
stylistic_characteristics: Free verse that keeps the cadences of talk: the poem as a record of the afternoon that produced it, with street names, shop windows, film stars and friends' names left in; the 'I do this, I do that' structure; surreal turns, camp jokes and sudden tenderness; an insistence that the poem is 'between two persons instead of two pages'.
intellectual_concerns: The city, the lunch hour and the ordinary day; friendship, love and gay desire; painting, music and the other arts, with painters as recurring heroes; the death of friends and of the famous, faced without ceremony; the belief that immediacy and speed are themselves values.
historical_significance: O'Hara is the central poet of the New York School and the model for the conversational, city-written American poem of the last half-century; the posthumous Collected Poems won the National Book Award, 'The Day Lady Died' and 'Why I Am Not a Painter' are among the most anthologised American poems of the period, and his manner - casual, fast, intimate, funny - is one of the dominant idioms of American poetry since 1960.
bibliographical_notes: The titles and dates above come from Wikipedia's article on O'Hara and its pages on Lunch Poems and Meditations in an Emergency, and from the Poetry Foundation's author page, read directly; they were not checked against a bibliography. Installment 10 records only the five Norton selections, 'Personism: A Manifesto' and four poems: the prose books and the contents of the posthumous volumes have no records, so the bibliography is incomplete.

birthplace: New York City, New York, United States
nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; poet, essayist and activist writing in English
literary_identity: American poet, essayist and self-described 'Black, lesbian, feminist, socialist, mother, warrior, poet', whose poems and essays on race, sexuality and the uses of anger and of the erotic made her a founding voice of Black feminist thought
biography: Audrey Geraldine Lorde was born in Harlem, New York, on 18 February 1934, the youngest of three daughters of immigrants from Barbados and Carriacou; she dropped the 'y' from her name as a child, learned to read at four and wrote her first poems at school, published a poem in Seventeen while still at Hunter High School, and took her BA at Hunter College and her MLS at Columbia. She worked as a librarian in New York and as a teacher, married the lawyer Edwin Rollins in 1962 and divorced in 1970, and had two children; she was active in the civil rights, anti-war, lesbian and feminist movements and was a founding member of Kitchen Table: Women of Color Press. The First Cities (1968), Cables to Rage (1970), From a Land Where Other People Live (1973, National Book Award finalist), New York Head Shop and Museum (1974), Coal (1976), The Black Unicorn (1978), Chosen Poems - Old and New (1982), Our Dead Behind Us (1986) and The Marvelous Arithmetics of Distance (1993) are the poetry; The Cancer Journals (1980), Zami: A New Spelling of My Name (1982), Sister Outsider (1984) and A Burst of Light (1988) the prose. She was Poet Laureate of New York State in 1991 and died at St Croix in the US Virgin Islands on 17 November 1992.
literary_profile: Poetry: The First Cities (1968), Cables to Rage (1970), From a Land Where Other People Live (1973), New York Head Shop and Museum (1974), Coal (1976), The Black Unicorn (1978), Chosen Poems - Old and New (1982), Our Dead Behind Us (1986) and The Marvelous Arithmetics of Distance (1993), gathered in The Collected Poems of Audre Lorde (1997). Prose: The Cancer Journals (1980), Zami: A New Spelling of My Name (1982), Sister Outsider: Essays and Speeches (1984), A Burst of Light (1988) and I Am Your Sister (2009).
stylistic_characteristics: A poetry of plain statement and long breath, often in loose free verse with biblical and incantatory repetition; anger and tenderness held in the same sentence; the first person used as a public voice; in the essays, a prose of direct address, short declarative paragraphs and aphorism ('the master's tools will never dismantle the master's house') that is meant to be spoken aloud.
intellectual_concerns: Race, racism and the struggle for civil rights, and the difference between them; sexuality, desire and the closet; gender, feminism and women's lives, above all the lives of Black women; the erotic as knowledge and power; illness, cancer and mortality; the uses of anger; poetry itself as a necessity rather than a luxury; the refusal of any hierarchy of oppressions.
historical_significance: Lorde is the central theoretician of intersectionality in Black feminist writing and one of the most widely quoted American essayists of the century; 'The Master's Tools Will Never Dismantle the Master's House' and 'Uses of the Erotic' are standard texts in women's, gender and Black studies, her Collected Poems is a landmark of American poetry, and her name is attached to institutions, prizes and reading rooms on several continents.
bibliographical_notes: The titles and dates above come from Wikipedia's articles on Lorde and on Sister Outsider, from the Library of Congress blog post on Chrysalis and from the contents listing of The Collected Poems in library catalogues, read directly; they were not checked against a bibliography. Installment 10 records only the five Norton selections - three poems, 'Coal', 'The Woman Thing' and 'Black Mother Woman', and two essays, 'Uses of the Erotic' and 'The Master's Tools'; the other books have no records, so the bibliography is incomplete.

birthplace: New York City, New York, United States
nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; essayist, novelist, playwright and film-maker writing in English
literary_identity: American essayist and public intellectual whose essays on interpretation, photography, illness and war - beginning with 'Against Interpretation' - made criticism itself a literary form and the critic a public figure
biography: Susan Sontag was born in New York on 16 January 1933, grew up on Long Island, in Tucson and in the San Fernando Valley, graduated from North Hollywood High School at fifteen, studied at Berkeley and at the University of Chicago and took an MA in philosophy at Harvard; she taught at Columbia and at City College, and her marriage to the sociologist Philip Rieff ended in 1959. 'Notes on "Camp"' in 1964 and the collection Against Interpretation (1966) made her famous as the critic who argued for the sensuous surface of art against the hunt for hidden meaning; Styles of Radical Will (1969), On Photography (1977), Illness as Metaphor (1978), Under the Sign of Saturn (1980), AIDS and Its Metaphors (1989), Regarding the Pain of Others (2003) and At the Same Time (2007) followed, with the novels The Benefactor (1963), Death Kit (1967), The Volcano Lover (1992) and In America (1999), the stories of I, etcetera (1978), the play Alice in Bed (1993) and the films Duet for Cannibals (1969) and Brother Carl (1971). She directed stage productions in besieged Sarajevo in 1993 and was awarded the Jerusalem Prize in 2001; she died in New York on 28 December 2004.
literary_profile: Non-fiction: Against Interpretation (1966), Styles of Radical Will (1969), On Photography (1977), Illness as Metaphor (1978), Under the Sign of Saturn (1980), AIDS and Its Metaphors (1989), Where the Stress Falls (2001) and Regarding the Pain of Others (2003), with the journals Reborn (2008) and As Consciousness Is Harnessed to Flesh (2012). Fiction: The Benefactor (1963), Death Kit (1967), I, etcetera (1978), The Volcano Lover (1992) and In America (1999). Plays and films: A Parsifal (1991), Alice in Bed (1993), Duet for Cannibals (1969) and Brother Carl (1971).
stylistic_characteristics: Aphoristic, declarative sentences in short numbered paragraphs; the essay built as a series of propositions rather than an argument with footnotes; a taste for lists, definitions and the imperative ('In place of a hermeneutics we need an erotics of art'); high and popular culture discussed in the same vocabulary; an authoritative first-person plural that speaks for the age.
intellectual_concerns: Interpretation and the critic's task; form against content; photography, images and the modern world; illness as metaphor and the metaphors we think with; war, atrocity and the ethics of looking at other people's suffering; camp, style and sensibility; the intellectual as a public figure.
historical_significance: Sontag is the most widely read American critic of the second half of the century and the writer who made the essay a public form; 'Against Interpretation' and 'Notes on "Camp"' are standard texts in criticism and cultural studies, On Photography and Illness as Metaphor shaped whole fields, and her name is a byword for the intellectual life of postwar New York.
bibliographical_notes: The titles and dates above come from Wikipedia's articles on Sontag and on Against Interpretation, read directly; they were not checked against a bibliography. Installment 10 records only the Norton selection, 'Against Interpretation' (Evergreen Review, December 1964; collected 1966); the other collections, the novels, the plays and the films have no records, so the bibliography is incomplete.
